body.objective: Students will be able to talk about activities with -er verbs.
body.iCan: I can talk about activities with -er verbs.
successCriteria: I can conjugate regular -er verbs in the present tense

body.hook: Most French verbs end in -er, and they all follow the same pattern. Learn one, like jouer or regarder, and you can use hundreds: danser, chanter, nager, skier…

study.title: Mes loisirs
study.question: How do I talk about my activities with -er verbs?
study.passage:
-er verb pattern (written for this lesson), using parler (to speak):
je parle, tu parles, il/elle/on parle, nous parlons, vous parlez, ils/elles parlent.
Endings: -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent. The -e, -es, -e and -ent forms all sound the same!
Text: Le week-end, je regarde des films et j'écoute de la musique. Ma sœur danse et chante. Mes amis et moi, nous nageons à la piscine. Mes parents regardent le hockey. Et vous, qu'est-ce que vous aimez faire ?
Frequency: toujours (always), souvent (often), parfois (sometimes), rarement (rarely), ne … jamais (never): Je ne danse jamais !
Activity: "Trouve quelqu'un qui…" (find someone who…): circulate and ask Tu nages souvent ? Tu chantes ? and write names.
study.source: Original text written for this lesson.
discussion: What does the family do on weekends?
What did you find out about classmates?
study.product: Write six sentences about leisure activities using different subject pronouns and three frequency words.

body.objective: Students will be able to use faire and jouer.
body.iCan: I can use faire and jouer.
successCriteria: I can use jouer à for sports and games and jouer de for instruments
I can use faire de for activities

body.hook: In English, you "play" soccer and "play" piano, and you "do" yoga. French makes the same kind of distinction with jouer à, jouer de and faire de, and the little words change with each activity.

vocabulary.definition: à + le / à + la / à + les
de + le / de + la / de + l'

study.title: Jouer ou faire ?
study.question: How do I talk about sports, games and instruments?
study.passage:
Guide (written for this lesson):
Faire (to do / make) is irregular: je fais, tu fais, il fait, nous faisons, vous faites, ils font.
jouer à + sport or game: à + le = au: Je joue au hockey. à + la = à la: Je joue à la balle. à + les = aux: Je joue aux cartes.
jouer de + instrument: de + le = du: Je joue du piano. de + la = de la: Je joue de la guitare.
faire de + activity: Je fais du vélo. Je fais de la natation. Je fais du ski. Je fais de l'escalade.
Canadian context: hockey and ringuette are popular across Canada; ringuette was invented in Ontario in 1963.
Activity: class survey: Tu fais du sport ? Tu joues d'un instrument ? Make a chart, then write five sentences about the class: Six élèves jouent au soccer…
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.
steps: Learn jouer à with au, à la, aux

body.objective: Students will be able to explore francophone culture in Canada.
body.iCan: I can explore francophone culture in Canada.
successCriteria: I can name francophone communities and celebrations in Canada
I can describe francophone culture in Alberta
I can compare a francophone tradition with my own
body.hook: French isn't just spoken in France. In Canada, about one in five people speak it as their first language, and there are francophone communities from Nova Scotia to British Columbia, including right here in Alberta.

study.title: Le Canada francophone
study.question: Where is French spoken in Canada, and how is it celebrated?
study.passage:
Background (written for this lesson from public sources):
French is one of Canada's two official languages. Quebec is the largest francophone province; New Brunswick is officially bilingual; there are francophone communities in every province and territory.
Francophone communities and celebrations: Quebec: la Fête nationale du Québec on 24 June; le Carnaval de Québec in winter. Acadie (New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, PEI): la Fête nationale de l'Acadie on 15 August with the noisy Tintamarre parade. Manitoba: le Festival du Voyageur in Winnipeg every February, celebrating fur-trade history.
Alberta: francophone communities include Bonnie Doon in Edmonton, Saint-Paul, Bonnyville, Falher, Legal, Plamondon and Beaumont. The University of Alberta's Campus Saint-Jean teaches in French. The Franco-Albertan flag (blue and white with a fleur-de-lis and a wild rose) was adopted in 1982.
Activities: 1. Map: mark francophone communities in Canada and Alberta. 2. Choose one celebration; find out when, where, what people do and what it celebrates. 3. Compare it with a celebration from your own family or culture in a Venn diagram, with French labels.
study.source: Summary from public sources about francophone communities in Canada and Alberta.
